ML based method · results · Digital twin: five years, 579 wells, Bengaluru-calibrated

What the forecaster achieved on the calibrated five-year twin.

Every number below is on the test year, August 2025 to July 2026: a forecast made every Monday for every well, compared with the twin's true (noise-free) water level. Levels are metres below ground. Days 1 and 7 use the operator's pumping plan for the coming week; on the twin the plan is the schedule that was then run. Weeks 4 and 12 use no plan. How the twin and the forecaster were built.

Typical miss, 7 days ahead0.24 m90 % within ±1 m
Typical miss, 4 weeks ahead0.39 m80 % within ±1 m
Typical miss, 12 weeks ahead0.70 m64 % within ±1 m

By horizon

The forecast against the true water level, for every forecast in the test year.

Typical miss: the median absolute difference between forecast and true level. Average miss: the mean. 8 in 10 within / 9 in 10 within: the distance from the true level that 80 % and 90 % of forecasts fall inside. Bias: predicted minus true, so a negative bias means the forecast puts the water higher than it is.

The typical forecast is within 0.18 m of the true level one day ahead, 0.24 m seven days ahead, 0.39 m four weeks ahead and 0.70 m twelve weeks ahead. Nine in ten forecasts are within ±0.71 m at day 1 and within ±1.01 m at day 7; eight in ten are within ±1.00 m at week 4 and ±1.54 m at week 12. Against an average depth to water of 89–94 m, the typical miss is 0.2 % of the depth at day 1 and 0.8 % at week 12, and the bias stays within ±0.2 m at every horizon. The 80 % bands contain 81–84 % of observed readings at days and 79–82 % at weeks; the 90 % bands contain 91–93 % and 90–92 %.

The forecast beside doing nothing

Doing nothing means the level stays where it was last seen. Forecasts where both are available.

Typical miss against the true level (m)

Share of forecasts within ±1 m of the true level (%)

What rain adds. With the calibrated monsoon, the rain inputs (past rain and the season's typical rain) lower the per-well mean error by 0.006–0.008 m at days 1 and 7, 0.01 m at one week and 0.05–0.07 m at 4–12 weeks. Replacing the season's typical rain with the rain that actually fell lowers it by a further 0.01 m at 12 weeks.

By well type

The same comparison for each of the six kinds of well. Pick a horizon.

Horizon

Typical miss against the true level (m), the forecast beside doing nothing

Forecast Doing nothing
  • Shallow valley wells are the most accurate at every horizon: a typical miss of 0.12 m at day 1 and 0.48 m at week 12, with 95 % of day-1 forecasts within half a metre.
  • Deep and low-yield wells miss more: 0.21–0.24 m at day 1 and 0.81–1.07 m at week 12.
  • Relative to depth, every type is close: the typical miss is under 2 % of the depth to water for every type and horizon — 1.07 m on a 160 m low-yield well at week 12.
  • Bias by type: within −0.08 to +0.18 m at days for every type; at 12 weeks shallow, mixed and deep-valley wells read 0.33–0.58 m high, deep-ridge and low-yield wells 0.27–0.44 m deep.

By season

Season is that of the date being forecast: monsoon June–October, post-monsoon November–January, dry February–May.

Horizon

Typical miss against the true level (m), the forecast beside doing nothing

Forecast Doing nothing
  • Season moves accuracy far less than horizon does: at each horizon the typical miss differs by a few centimetres between seasons — 0.17–0.18 m at day 1, 0.23–0.25 m at day 7, 0.37–0.42 m at week 4, 0.65–0.79 m at week 12.
  • Post-monsoon is the hardest season at weeks (0.79 m typical miss at week 12), and at day 7 the forecast reads 0.28 m deep there while monsoon recharge keeps arriving through each well's 5–30-day delay.
  • The dry season has the smallest typical miss at day 1, week 4 and week 12 (0.17, 0.37 and 0.65 m).

Stress tests

Both tests are one change from the reference twin — the typed, paved twin before the recharge calibration (how they were built). Errors are per-well mean (median) against the observed resting level, in metres; daily with the plan, weekly without.

A non-linearity the physics does not contain: quadratic well loss

The quadratic term takes the physics core's fit out of its depth, yet the forecast error fell at every horizon and the bands held.

Per-well mean error by horizon (m)

Reference twin: wells follow the core's linear law Same twin with a quadratic well loss C·Q² in every well

The quadratic term takes the physics core's fit out of its depth: the fitted refill time no longer ranks the wells (rank correlation −0.08, from 0.83), and the fitted drawdown coefficient comes out eight times the true one. The forecast error did not rise. It fell at every horizon — by 0.02–0.05 m on the per-well mean and by up to 0.06 m for the typical well — and the bands held. With the core's parameters no longer physical, the learning layer, trained on the same records, carried the forecast: the system absorbed a non-linear relationship that its physics core does not contain. Weekly errors are scored on the same weekly target in both twins; level noise ±0.2 m.

Neighbour interference: the counterfactual

The existing models scored on the reference twin with its neighbour links and on the same twin with the links switched off. Oracle, not deployable.

A negative difference means the models forecast the world without neighbours worse. Switching the links off moves the true resting level by 5.9 m on average over the test year (95th percentile 24.8 m; shallow kinds 2.0–2.5 m, deep kinds 6.2–9.3 m). Level noise ±0.2 m.

  • Interference is a large part of where a well's level sits — 5.9 m on average — yet it is not left over as forecast error. At day 7 the typical well's error is the same with and without neighbours (0.34 m).
  • The models forecast the world without neighbours worse, by 0.13 m at day 7 and 0.36 m at 12 weeks: they learned each well together with its neighbours, through the per-well physics fit and the well's own recent history. The models built for unseen wells, which carry no per-well memory, change by 0.07 m at day 7 and at 12 weeks.
  • Per kind at 12 weeks the difference is −0.09 m (SW-V), −0.14 m (SW-R), −0.20 m (MX), −0.41 m (DF-V), −0.49 m (DF-R) and −0.50 m (LY): the deeper and better-connected the kind, the more the models carry their neighbours.
Where every number comes from

Every figure on this page is on the twin, with ±0.2 m level noise. No real level measurement was used. Iteration 1 of this page is kept as a record.

What real data would change →

Borewell Forecast is a proof of concept for forecasting groundwater levels in Bengaluru borewells. Results are labelled by where the data came from: vendor export (15 days, July 2026, in the vendor's real format but with demonstration water-level values), synthetic test system (450 simulated wells with a known answer) or digital twin (physics-based simulations of the 579 wells: one year in iteration 1, five years in later iterations and in Stage 2). No real water-level measurement has been used yet, and nothing here is yet a validated field forecast. Built by the FARII consortium.
